correctness.rationale: Induction gives R-linear coefficient terms summing to I. The critical binary-term closure lemma is proved using finite injective affine coefficient maps, translations by U(C-C), and generation of R by T and 1. Thus every r in R occurs, not merely every image bound. Principal ideal structure reduces arbitrary equation images to rV; primary decomposition gives sizes and the irreducibility boundary. Six full finite checks cover 27,318 direct pair evaluations but are corroborative, not infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The 2026 general classification arXiv:2610.37841 covers minimal spectra and generic affine finiteness/image bounds; these prior facts are acknowledged and are not claimed novel. The precise full spectrum for the one-operation latin Alexander quandle, constructive realization by two-variable terms, and elementary-divisor set formula are not stated or implied by the checked results without a further term-clone argument. Actual published-finding corpus and literature searches found no covering prior theorem, subject to residual risk of historical term-clone equivalence.
residual_risks: A classical affine/quasigroup term-clone theorem may make the coefficient-reachability argument already known, although an explicit probability-spectrum consequence was not located.
General 2026 minimal-spectrum classifications already imply broader statements, so novelty must be confined to full attainable rank spectra and binary witnesses.
Search results are not an exhaustive literature proof; secondary references and other languages may contain equivalent expressions.

value.rationale: It answers the precise all-equations spectrum question for a significant natural infinite family of nonassociative latin quandles, gives exact attainable probabilities for arbitrary elementary divisors, and separates irreducible, split, and repeated-primary cases. The reverse-attainability lemma yields more information than generic finite-spectrum or minimality theorems; the result is independently motivated by 2026 published equational-probability research.
